text:
A mangrove can protect a port. A wetland can reduce pressure on a drainage system. A restored floodplain can lower flood risk to roads and communities.

Yet these systems are still often funded as environmental projects beside infrastructure, rather than managed as part of the infrastructure service itself.

A World Bank, World Resources Institute and African Development Bank review identified nearly 300 nature-based-solution projects in Sub-Saharan Africa, with cumulative funding above US$21 billion between 2012 and 2023.

The financial case can be strong. The Global Center on Adaptation reports that well-designed nature-based solutions can produce benefit-cost ratios of 2:1 to 8:1. But those are portfolio-level ranges, not guaranteed returns for an individual project.

The harder question is whether a living system is designed to deliver a measurable protective service over time.

A seawall normally has a specification, an owner, an inspection regime and a maintenance budget. A mangrove belt protecting it may have none of those things. It can sit across several landholdings, depend on community use and ecological conditions, and be funded only until a restoration grant ends.

StoneComms' conclusion is that nature-based protection needs the same institutional discipline as the engineered asset it supports.

We propose a six-part Living Infrastructure Contract:

HAZARD — what physical risk is changing?
SERVICE — what protection must the living system deliver?
BOUNDARY — where does the asset begin, and whose land, rights and livelihoods are inside it?
STEWARD — who is accountable after establishment?
FINANCE — what pays for preparation, monitoring and long-term management?
PROOF — how will protective performance and fairness be verified?

This does not mean nature should replace concrete. In many projects the strongest design will combine both. Mangroves can reduce wave energy before a seawall takes the remaining load. Wetlands can store water before drains carry extreme flows. Vegetation can stabilise slopes while engineered structures protect critical points.

Community impacts also belong inside the infrastructure case. If people lose access to land, fishing, grazing or other livelihoods so that a protective ecosystem can function, those costs cannot be treated as an environmental side issue.

The investment question should therefore move beyond “how many hectares were restored?”

What service must this system deliver, who will maintain it, who bears the cost, and how will we know it is still protecting people and assets years after the project opens?
